A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MMTutorBench. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison. Existing material can be matched across the expanded and renumbered appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 12 MLLMs, human and Study Mode comparisons, input ablations, judge-validation results and error analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds empirical human-validation, persona-adaptability, multi-turn, weighted-scoring and subgroup analyses.

M1.justification: The core video-to-key-step construction pipeline, context reconstruction, three-part tutoring output and six-dimensional rubric remain unchanged. The additions extend evaluation scenarios and scoring protocols; they do not introduce a new tutor model or revise the core tutoring algorithm.

E1.justification: V2 adds simulated multi-turn tutoring with progressive, exploratory and introspective queries, plus novice/anxious and advanced/focused persona scenarios (Section 3.2; Appendices D and H). These introduce sustained scaffolding and adaptation requirements beyond v1's single-turn coverage.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds a Standard Judge comparator and removes ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 from the reported comparison. Appendix C.2 further evaluates the rubric-free judge. The main twelve-model roster is retained; expanded model names and the corrected open-source model count do not establish changed membership.

E3.justification: The reported benchmark grows from 685 to 770 problems. New protocols include a 100-instance human-validation set deliberately oversampling hard cases, persona-conditioned evaluation with binary Adaptivity Alignment, and weighted rubric aggregation. Multi-turn evaluation reports 168 second-turn and 82 third-turn instances (Appendices C–E and H).

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of judge agreement by domain and difficulty, sensitivity to rubric weights, model performance across domains and difficulty levels, persona adaptation, and scaffolding across dialogue turns. Existing input ablations and the original case study remain, with the latter relocated from Appendix E to I.

E5.justification: Appendix A.1 newly reports dual-blind annotation on 10% of the data and inter-annotator agreement above 90%, adding statistical reliability reporting. Neither version provides repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests for model performance; additional Pearson-correlation rows alone do not establish such improvements.

E6.justification: Table 3 scores change throughout: Gemini-2.5-Pro changes from 4.77 to 4.69 and Qwen2.5-VL-72B from 3.45 to 3.40. The benchmark also changes, preventing same-setting performance interpretations. V2 adds extensive results, including human correlations of 0.8926 versus 0.4487 for the rubric-based and standard judges (Table 8). Figure 6 changes the reported Hard proportion from 71.4% to 5.6%.

T1.justification: The SSIM-based scene-boundary equations in Appendix A.2 are unchanged. Neither version adds theoretical guarantees or proofs. The new scoring weights and empirical evaluation criteria do not introduce substantive mathematical theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions and claims: a multimodal tutoring benchmark with three tasks and six rubric dimensions, proprietary/open-source and human/model gaps, OCR degradation, limited few-shot gains and reliable rubric-based judging. The updated benchmark size does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations involving behavioral rigidity under persona instructions, deteriorating scope control across turns, geometry-related visual reasoning weaknesses and robustness to rubric weighting. Its limitations replace the single-turn restriction with an explicit qualification about simulated questions failing to capture authentic learner language and spontaneity.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code/data repository link and substantially expands documentation through curation rejection/correction rates, persona instructions, the adaptivity rubric, weighting specifications and difficulty definitions. It also identifies the primary judge and describes the inter-judge subset. These are documented details and access information, without establishing that previously reported procedures were changed.

R1.justification: The reference lists contain the same works, and the related-work discussion retains the same positioning against text-based tutoring and multimodal problem-solving benchmarks. No substantive new relationship to prior research is introduced.

P1.justification: V2 condenses and rewrites portions of the experimental discussion, corrects author affiliations and model descriptions, clarifies optional student queries, and reorganizes the expanded appendices. Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain recognizable; the added scientific material does not constitute a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 7–18 for curation, validation, persona instructions, scoring and supplementary results. Figure 2 gains a dynamic-interaction component, Table 6 gains comparator categories, and Figure 6 revises its domain labels and distributions. Existing validation and case-study figures are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens validation with a rubric-free judge comparator, stratified human correlations and quantified curation checks, while adding useful tutoring analyses and code/data access information. These gains support a limited net improvement. Important qualifications remain: Table 18 has only five introspective examples, and Table 14's weighted scores appear consistent with v1's components rather than v2's updated Table 3, leaving their evaluation basis unclear.
